items.author: rdmuser
items.content:
We are proud to announce something that our small team of very dedicated people at Kagi has been building for a long time – the . A private email and calendar with a @kagimail.com address, or with your own domains.

If you’ve already swapped Google Search for Kagi and Chrome for Orion, your inbox is probably the last big piece of your digital life still at Google. Now you can move that too.

Does the world need another email service? We asked ourselves that question more than once. There are great ones out there, and we’re fans of what Fastmail and Tuta are doing. We still built our own, for the same reason we build everything at Kagi: technology should do its job and then get out of your way.

For email, that job is to be fast, private, and secure. On top of that, it should help you stay on track with what’s important: bring forward what you need to act on, respond to, or acknowledge, and quietly handle the rest.

Kagi Mail also has to treat you the way Kagi Search and Orion do: no surveillance, no ads, open standards, and no lock-in.

Kagi Mail is included in . Sign in with your Kagi account, and you’re set. AI features draw from your existing Allowance. On another plan, or no Kagi account yet? After the free 60-day trial, you can get Kagi Mail for $99/year (+ Sales Tax).

How it works: A service and a client, on open standards

To deliver the experience we believe in, we built the full stack: hosting for your addresses and domains, plus the mail and calendar apps. It runs on open standards and open-source infrastructure (the Stalwart server, IMAP, JMAP, and CalDAV), so you can use Kagi’s apps or any compatible client you already like.

  • Organize your mail in your own words. Brief it the way you’d brief an assistant: “Label anything where beta users send product feedback. It might come from @kagimail.com, but use judgment.” You decide what permissions each rule gets (read the content, or skip the inbox).
  • show what needs you today, and learn from what you dismiss.
  • in plain language and get direct answers with the source email, including text inside scanned PDFs and photos.
  • reads newsletters like a feed, out of the way of real mail.
  • Tracking pixels and remote images are blocked or proxied, so senders can’t tell when or where you opened their mail.
  • Sender screening holds new senders until you approve them, so they never reach your inbox uninvited.
  • Suspicious senders trigger a phishing warning, while verified senders show their (BMI) logo.

No ads, ever. No profiling, no selling, no sharing your data.

  • Shared addresses on your domain (team@, info@, family@): create an alias, then choose which people have access to it
  • Sign in through a social login, or your organization’s own identity provider (OIDC)
  • Shared mailboxes
  • Kagi Translate is built in
  • Write to assistant@kagimail.com for answers about your mail (actions coming soon)
  • Proofread and translation included while you write emails

For power users and developers

  • command palette, shortcuts, and search operators
  • Rule-based filtering with Sieve, no AI involved
  • MCP server with read access to your mail
  • Works with Apple Mail, Thunderbird, and any IMAP/JMAP/CalDAV client, with automatic setup

We will keep adding new capabilities – here’s what to expect over the next few quarters.

Until the mobile apps arrive, use the mobile web app or any IMAP/JMAP client, such as Apple Mail or Thunderbird.

Our “no lock-in” promise to you

Leaving Kagi Mail is as easy as joining it. Your mail, calendar, and workflows are yours, and you can export them at any time, through standard protocols and a one-click export experience. You’ll keep access to your mailbox for six months after leaving Kagi Mail. You can send and receive emails for the first 60 days, then read and export your mail with one click for the remaining four months. We build an ecosystem so things work better together for those who want it, not to trap anyone.

We want Kagi Mail to be the first email account we’d create for our children. We’re not there yet, but it is a high bar we hold ourselves to, and every feature in this beta is a step toward it: a calm, safe place to communicate, and a window onto an internet that treats you as a person, not a product who’s been tracked, targeted, and sold to.

We can build it this way because of you. Kagi has no ad business, and no one pushing us to monetize your inbox; you’re not a dataset for ads or AI. You are here because you believe the internet can be built differently. Thank you.

items.title: Ladybird is now in alpha
items.author: janvdberg
items.content:
Hello friends! Ladybird is now in alpha. You can download it for macOS and Linux.

I’ve been looking forward to writing this post for a long time. :^)

Ladybird is a browser with a new engine. The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork. The browser around it is modest, but functional.

This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details.

We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird!

The alpha is a rolling channel, and we’ll be pushing out automatic updates regularly. This is the part I’m most excited about. Ladybird improves quickly, and until now you had to build it from source to see that.

If you build websites, try yours in Ladybird and tell us what breaks. It supports WebDriver for automated testing, as well as the Firefox DevTools protocol.

Thank you to our sponsors and donors, and to everyone who has tested, reported bugs, and written code over the years. There’s still a mountain of work ahead of us, but I’m very happy that you can finally try Ladybird for yourself!

items.title: Kubernetes v1.38 Sneak Peek
items.content:
As we get closer to the release date for Kubernetes v1.38, the project develops and matures, features may be deprecated, removed, or replaced with better ones for the project's overall health. This blog post outlines some of the planned changes for the Kubernetes v1.38 release that the release team feels you should be aware of for the continued maintenance of your Kubernetes environment and keeping up to date with the latest changes. The information listed below is based on the current status of the v1.38 release and may change before the actual release date.

Deprecations and removals for Kubernetes v1.38

kubectl: WebSocket opt-out environment variables removed

has used WebSockets instead of SPDY by default for , and since v1.30, and for since v1.31. The KUBECTL_REMOTE_COMMAND_WEBSOCKETS and KUBECTL_PORT_FORWARD_WEBSOCKETS environment variables let you turn that behavior off. These variables are going to be removed in v1.38. will then always try WebSockets first and fall back to SPDY when it needs to (the same as the current default behavior). If your scripts or CI environments set either of these environment variables, you can remove them since they will no longer have any effect.

kubectl: dropped from kuberc credential plugin allowlist entries

The file keeps kubectl user preferences separate from cluster credentials in the kubeconfig, including an allowlist of the credential plugins is allowed to run. In the beta kubectl.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 API, an allowlist entry can use as an alias for . The field (not ) has been deprecated since v1.36.

With expected to graduate to stable in v1.38, the new API will not include . If any of your allowlist entries use , change them to now.

Future removal of cgroup v1 support

Support for cgroup v1 is being phased out. Since v1.35, the kubelet fails to start on nodes that use cgroup v1 unless you set in the kubelet configuration. This option remains available in v1.38, but it should be treated as a short-term fix as support for cgroup v1 is planned to be removed in a future release. If you haven't already, please plan your migration to cgroup v2.

Admission webhooks no longer receive authentication and authorization review requests

Since v1.37, the ExcludeAdmissionWebhookVirtualResources feature gate has been enabled by default. With it on, validating and mutating admission webhooks no longer receive requests for (virtual) writes to TokenReview, SelfSubjectReview, SubjectAccessReview, SelfSubjectAccessReview, LocalSubjectAccessReview or SelfSubjectRulesReview. Creating or updating a webhook configuration whose rules name one of these resources returns a deprecation warning, and the API server logs any existing configurations that are affected when it starts.

If you rely on a webhook to see these requests, you can turn the feature gate off for now, but note that the gate is planned to be locked on when the feature graduates to stable.

Breaking changes in Kubernetes v1.38

Container runtimes must report the cgroup driver

The kubelet in v1.37 and older supported releases provides a legacy mechanism to configure the cgroup driver. The modern way to do that is via the CRI RPC, which reports the cgroup driver that the container runtime recommends using. In v1.38, the kubelet defaults to not allowing the legacy configuration mechanism: it will be both deprecated and unavailable unless explicitly re-activated. As a result, v1.38 nodes will essentially require that your container runtime is running the kubelet starts (to look up the expected cgroup driver); if the kubelet can't get the cgroup driver from the runtime even after retrying, it will exit with an error before even registering the node.

As part of this upcoming release, the field in the kubelet configuration file will be deprecated. Not only is specifying that field going to be deprecated, the kubelet will actually reject it unless you reactivate the legacy mechanism by enabling the (temporary) LegacyCgroupDriverFallback feature gate. The kubeadm tool will also no longer set to by default, and its preflight checks will report an error if the runtime doesn't support the RPC. If any of your nodes run an older, incompatible container runtime, you should follow the instructions in the official v1.38 release notes about how to upgrade.

Pod-level resources: swap behavior changes on nodes

If you use pod-level resources on Linux nodes that use cgroup v2 and are configured with , the kubelet in v1.38 will start applying swap limits based on the Pod's pod-level memory settings. This means that Pods whose pod-level memory request equals their memory limit will get no swap at all (both for the Pod and for every container in it), even if a container sets a memory request lower than its limit. Check any workloads that rely on swap before you upgrade, and be sure to read the official release notes for v1.38 for detailed advice.

Featured enhancements of Kubernetes v1.38

The following list of enhancements is likely to be included in the upcoming v1.38 release. This is not a commitment and the release content is subject to change.

kubectl user preferences (kuberc) graduating to stable

kuberc, the separate kubectl configuration file for user preferences such as aliases, default options and a credential plugin policy, is expected to graduate to stable in v1.38.

Pod-level resources graduating to stable

Pod-level resources, which let you set CPU, memory and hugepages requests and limits for a Pod as a whole, are expected to graduate to stable in v1.38. If you run Linux nodes with , see the swap behavior change above before you upgrade.

DRA support for partitionable devices graduating to stable

Partitionable devices let a Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) driver advertise a device such as a GPU both as a whole and as smaller partitions, and the scheduler allocates only combinations that fit within the physical device. The feature is expected to graduate to stable in v1.38, and the feature gate will then be locked on.

EvictionRequest API (alpha)

Evicting a Pod isn’t always as simple as terminating it. Some applications may be in the middle of important work, such as data migration or cleanup, and terminating them without giving them time to prepare can cause disruptions.

The EvictionRequest API introduces a more coordinated way to evict Pods. It gives applications and controllers time to prepare before a Pod is evicted. For example, when a node needs to be drained or a Pod needs to be moved to another node, a controller can create an EvictionRequest to signal that this Pod needs to be evicted.

The eviction request controller coordinates with the responders configured for the Pod. These responders can perform application-specific tasks such as completing ongoing work, cleaning up resources, or migrating data before the Pod is terminated.

If no custom responder is available or responders don't complete the process, Kubernetes can fall back to the existing API-initiated eviction mechanism, which continues to respect PodDisruptionBudgets (PDBs). The EvictionRequest API does not replace PDBs. It gives applications a chance to participate in the eviction process.

As this is an alpha feature, you will need to enable the feature gate the relevant alpha API group. Check the v1.38 release notes and documentation, once they're available, to confirm exactly what's required.

New features and deprecations are also announced in the Kubernetes release notes. We will formally announce what's new in Kubernetes v1.38 as part of the CHANGELOG for that release.

The Kubernetes v1.38 release is planned for Wednesday, December 16th, 2026. Stay tuned for updates!

You can see the announcements of changes in the release notes for:

The simplest way to get involved with Kubernetes is by joining one of the many Special Interest Groups (SIGs) that align with your interests.

If you don't know where to start, join our monthly New Contributor Orientations where we teach the community how the project is structured, and we'll guide you on how to make your first contribution to the project.

items.title: Jensen Huang Reinstated as Nvidia CEO
items.author: alanwong
items.content:
NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) today announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.

“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.” Harvey Jones will remain as Board chair.

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Jensen Huang. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.” 

As previously announced, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation. The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.

The Board also recently formed a National Security and Export Control Committee comprised solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. The committee is engaging counsel with experience in national security matters, and such counsel will be retaining advisors with expertise in national security matters. NVIDIA is commencing a search to fill a new position, Chief Compliance Officer, to oversee compliance across NVIDIA and report to the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. NVIDIA will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries.

items.title: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
items.author: jaz
items.content:
The board of directors said it unanimously voted to reinstate Huang following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him. The board added that it "received input from senior levels of the United States government" and that it is confident Huang's reinstatement "poses no national security risk."

President Donald Trumptold CNBC on Monday that he had been speaking to Nvidia's board "directly and indirectly," and that Huang "did nothing wrong." Trump said he talked to Huang on Sunday and asked him to promise to "work hard."

Huang resigned from his role as chief executive earlier this month after a series of shocking reports about multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. The New York Times reported on Sunday that the woman, Alice Huang, was in contact with an officer of China's Ministry of State Security during at least part of the time that she was engaging in a relationship with Huang.

Shares of Nvidia surged 33% following Huang's reinstatement. The stock had shed nearly 33% from the time Huang admitted to an extramarital affair on Nov. 8. The stock closed at $186.64 on Nov.6.

"I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in a statement. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process."

Senior government officials briefed Nvidia's board late last week and communicated that no national security laws were violated, according to sources familiar with the discussion who asked to remain anonymous because they were not authorized to speak publicly. That update prompted the board to reach out to Huang, the people said.

Huang and the board held their first conversations since his ouster on Saturday, and the group determined he would return as CEO during a second meeting on Sunday, the people said. Nvidia's cratering stock price played a role in accelerating those conversations.

Trump celebrated Huang's return to Nvidia on Monday, writing in a post on his social media site that the board made "the correct and proper decision" to reinstate him. Trump said the U.S. needs Huang's leadership to "ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy."

He reiterated that the U.S. government has "no reason to believe" Huang's return poses a risk to national security, and that it "does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."

"On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure," Trump wrote.

Several tech industry leaders, including Elon Musk, CEO of , Gavin Baker, managing partner and chief investment officer at Atreides Management, and Brad Gerstner, Altimeter Capital CEO, had been actively lobbying for Huang's return. Musk wrote in a post on X on Monday that the board's "mistake has been corrected."

Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

For weeks following Huang's ouster, the company's board maintained that it was not considering Huang's reinstatement. It appointed Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, as the chipmaker's interim CEO, who reiterated that position in an interview with CNBC following Huang's exit. Kress will continue to serve as Nvidia's CFO, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Nvidia's board formed an independent committee and hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an investigation into Huang and whether company secrets or national security were compromised. The board said Monday that "the committee's investigation will proceed to conclusion" and that Huang is "committed to cooperating with it."

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Nvidia's board chair, Harvey Jones, said in a statement. "We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company."

Even with Huang back at the helm, Nvidia is facing increased scrutiny over its chip sales in Southeast Asia and China.

Lawmakers have been preparing for investigations into how Huang's affair with the alleged spy may have damaged U.S. AI dominance, influenced his positions on export controls, and impacted his close relationships with Trump and his Cabinet. Huang has been one of the loudest voices opposing strict export controls on advanced chips.

"The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., said in a statement Monday.

Huang is due for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, is scheduled to appear before the panels on Dec. 2. Those dates were set before Huang's return, and John Fisher, who represents Huang, did not comment on whether there are any changes in his plans to testify.

Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C., said Monday that Huang will publicly testify on Dec. 3 as the sole witness during a hearing titled, "Protecting America's AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls."

"Americans deserve answers about what NVIDIA and the Trump administration knew, when they knew it, and whether sufficient steps were taken to prevent sensitive technology from falling into the wrong hands," Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., a member of the Banking Committee, wrote in a post on X on Monday.

items.title: The next circle of security hell
items.author: qtqtqt
items.content:
A few years back I wrote “The modern packager’s security nightmare”. Have things improved since? On the contrary, I feel like we’re slipping down a well-oiled slope with no end in sight. Vulnerabilities are reported at unprecedented rates. A lot of people are doing everything they can to patch them up, which doesn’t necessarily mean they’re not making things even worse. Complex software involves complex trees of dependencies, and every branch on that tree needs tending to. When they stop being reliable, people further down the tree start taking more weight. And there’s a limit of how much a single person can do, so what started as an effort to resolve an issue upstream may quickly become a weakness. Is software less secure these days? It’s tempting to say yes. I’d love to blame the corporate sector for egotistically dumping low quality software on us. I’d love to blame marketing-oriented people developing stuff with the sole goal of making a profit. I’d love to blame Rust for getting people obsessed about memory safety, and ignoring the kinds of vulnerabilities that aren’t caught by the compiler. Finally, I’d really love to blame slop. But the truth is, I don’t know. That’s really beside the point.

The point is that nowadays everyone and their chatbot became security researchers. Projects are being flooded with vulnerability reports. Even though pretty much every bug bounty was discontinued because of slop, people aren’t stopping. And even if we disregard truly invalid junk reports, there’s a lot left, and you have to deal with them somehow. You have to figure out how important they are, and how to fix them (or more likely, whether the fixes submitted are truly valid and don’t introduce regressions), or if you should reject them and why.

In the end, security is tricky. We’re seeing lots of bugs like REDoS, or other kinds of “performance bugs”. Are they really vulnerabilities? Well, it depends on the attack vector. And that in turn depends on how the software is used. Some scenarios are really contrived, and feel like “shell can execute dangerous commands if you type them in”. But then, you also have really serious issues such as “timing attack can be used to guess user’s secret”. You need to know a lot to make that kind of judgment, and sometimes your judgment doesn’t really match users’ expectations.

In the end, what can project maintainers do? Even if they have the expertise and the energy to judge, if they can “know better”, there’s likely a CVE assigned already. It may have absurdly high score. All security scanners will complain unless you fix it, and users will come asking or complaining, or attacking, or forking. I mean, technology can’t handle nuances. More than once I’ve been doing unnecessary security stabilizations over vulnerabilities that didn’t affect Gentoo (for example, because we already unbundled the vulnerable dependencies), to avoid false positives from security scanners. I’ve been also doing meaningless version bumps (with no real changes or no changes that applied to Gentoo) so that our packages don’t get reported as being “outdated”. It’s a hassle and it sucks, but it saves people from worrying.

I’ve said this before and I’ll say it again: most projects aren’t really prepared to handle security issues. And it’s not just about triage. It’s about having LTS or security branches, it’s about making proper security releases with minimal changes. Unfortunately, it’s quite common for security fixes to be combined with new features, deprecations, API changes. In extreme cases, people are caught with their metaphorical pants down, and suddenly need to make a security release in the middle of a major rewrite, or along with barely tested new code. And then, people downstream discover that they need to quickly deal with major API changes to upgrade past a vulnerable version. These things keep piling up.

What happens next? The community reaches a breaking point. People can’t keep up. You discover you can’t rely on others, so you work around them. You start bundling more stuff. Soon enough your workload goes beyond your ability. Software development becomes “every chatbot for itself”. The nightmare becomes worse, and the wheel keeps turning.

items.title: Don't keep your SSH keys on disk
items.author: shintoist
items.content:
Although it's clear to me that some of the panic is unwarranted, all the recent security vulnerability reports and company breaches are a good reason to think about what you're doing to avoid risk, and to mitigate exposure if something bad happens.

I'm a pathological self-hoster and I've been running all kinds of systems, from old toy projects to fun tools, and over time I've accumulated a lot of them. This has changed in the last couple of months, where I've instead been pruning my running services. I've taken down unused old apps, because anything can be an entry point into your system. And they were anyway. I've also moved most of services behind my Tailscale, with some judicious use of to poke little holes for specific things that do need to be publicly accessible. And I've been obssessively updating everything on my servers that can be updated.

That brings us to my personal computer. I've been trying to do the same kind of due diligence that I did for my servers, on my personal devices. I have been a long time user of password managers, and I recently wrote about moving to Bitwarden, and I am careful to always enable 2FA or passkeys on every service I use. But one area I've fallen behind is .

A better approach to SSH keys

I was keeping copies of my private keys in my password manager, for safe-keeping, but I was still using the version on disk, loaded into memory with . To just make this absolutely clear, this means that the private keys are vulnerable to be exiltrated by malicious code scanning my disk. After reading articles like I deleted all my SSH keys, I finally decided to take the next step and get them off disk.

I knew that for this to work for me, it had to be easy to use and the disruption had to be minimal, and so although things like the OSX Secure Enclave sounds incredibly cool, I needed something with better ergonomics. I already had Bitwarden set up, with the keys in it, and so that's the approach I ended up taking, and it has worked great for me.

Setting up the Bitwarden SSH agent

Ok, let's go through the steps. First, make sure your private keys are in Bitwarden. If they are not, you'll want to import them. Note that the Bitwarden UI for importing SSH keys is a bit awkward.

  1. Create a new SSH key in Bitwarden, it'll automatically generate one for you.
  2. Copy your existing private key into your clipboard, eg cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa | pbcopy.
  3. On the Private Key header in the edit form, at the very far right of the asterisks hiding the value, there's an upload icon, click it.
  4. Your private key has been imported. Give it a good name and save.

Once you're done with that, you can now move on to the next step, which is enabling the Bitwarden SSH agent. Note that these instructions are for the direct install, if you installed it through the App Store I think the path is different. Go to Preferences, App settings (all accounts), and find the checkbox for "Enable SSH agent". You'll also get the option of choosing how often it prompts you for permission, when something wants to use the key. I went for whenever the vault is locked, which I have set to every 4 hours, balancing security with convenience.

Next, add to your file:

This tells to use the Bitwarden SSH agent. This applies globally, so anything that calls should now check the agent. Separately, you'll want to add this to your terminal config file, eg :

This ensures anything that needs the SSH agent in your terminal, that isn't , also go to the right place. This covers tools like . Okay, now try it out with . This should list all the keys loaded into . If you're confident you've copied all of your keys into your password manager, you can now delete the ones on disk.

Bonus: git commit signing

Git commits traditionally contain author information, but no proof that the author is who they say they are. This means it's trivial to impersonate someone else in a commit. It's still mitigated by the fact that git repositories generally have access controls, so a third party would not be able to push commits in the first place, but there is also a mechanism available for proving that the git originated from the claimed author: commit signing.

In the past, this was limited to GPG keys, but modern git supports signing using SSH keys. So I've set this up too, using a dedicated key that only has that job. This means that creating the commit and pushing it to the repo requires separate SSH keys, and each one has to be authorized separately.

Go to a repo and create a commit, then run , and you should see your signature there.

To have forges recognize your signature you have to teach them what it is. For Github that means going to https://github.com/settings/keys and adding it as a signing key. Tangled automatically trusts your configured SSH keys as signing keys. Gitea and Forgejo require some extra steps to trust your key, just follow their instructions at .

My experience after a couple of weeks

I've adjusted quickly. Everything just works out of the box, the only added friction is that now and then Bitwarden prompts me for permission to use keys, which if it's unlocked just means clicking "approve" on a dialog. If it's locked, I can unlock it with touch ID.

If any Bitwarden employees happen to be reading this, it would be nice if instead of clicking approve, I could use touch ID to approve use of the key. Or at least by hitting enter. As it is, I always have to move to the touchpad to approve. It would also be great if I could separately configure the vault lock interval and the same interval for keys. But that's just minor requests, overall it works just great for me, and it's not too disruptive.

And now I get to sleep a bit easier!

items.title: Yes, 17M lines of Lean is a lot
items.author: seizethecheese
items.content:
AI disclosure: I wrote all text here, but used Agent Duel (an open source battle system on top of OpenCode) to research sources of Lean proofs and generate charts.

The recent proof of the Riemann hypothesis came with a statistic attached: the proof is 17 million lines of Lean. Beyond the philosophical questions of what it means to have a proof longer than any human could comprehend, I’m left with a simpler question: is that as large as it sounds?

To investigate, I hunted for collections of Lean proofs online. I found two and charted the lengths of their proofs.

(All charts have a log x axis, which makes 17m lines look a lot closer to 1m and 100k than it really is.)

Famous theorems in Mathlib

Mathlib maintains a collection of famous proofs. There are over 1k but only 259 have Lean associated, which I chart here.

These are all human generated, and as we can see, they come nowhere close to 17m.

Every Lean package on Reservoir

Reservoir indexes every published Lean package, 938 of which have Lean code on GitHub. This one has a lot more data, including AI assisted proofs. We even have a few that are over 16m!:

  1. this appears to be an AI built proof that is still a work in progress.

  2. , a project linking the LMFDB database of number theory objects to Mathlib. This isn’t really a proof: about 98% of its Lean is files generated by scripts that check the database’s numbers one by one. The hand-written part is closer to 500k lines.

  3. is another Anthropic special: a complete proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem, published on GitHub in September. Its README says “the Lean sources were produced by AI agents building on human-written open-source Lean”, including the human FLT project led by Kevin Buzzard, which is about 60k lines and still in progress. The AI version is roughly 450 times longer.

So yes, 17m lines is a lot.

items.title: A Beginner's Guide to Local AI with Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth
items.author: Retell15
items.content:
With the launch of open-weight models like Qwen, cloud-based LLM providers seem like they're more of infrastructure or appliance businesses when it comes to most routine tasks that an AI model can handle.

OpenAI and Anthropic have displayed a pattern of dropping model quality in the 'latest' version and controlling exactly what you're allowed to run on their models. Add to this ballooning costs and privacy concerns, and we get a pretty good case for moving away from this 'convenient' cloud experience.

That's basically where I was too. I wanted to offload certain token-heavy research, data collection, or coding tasks to an AI model without staring at usage limits all day. So, as any reasonable human being would do, I decided to set up my own local AI: a Claude and ChatGPT replacement that runs at home on my own hardware.

Since this was my first attempt, my primary focus was keeping it simple and hosting it on Windows. If you're a beginner, you can follow along to get one going on your home network too.

Once you have the hardware sorted, it takes about 10-15 minutes (excluding download times).

Install Unsloth Desktop, download a quantized AI model that fits your GPU's VRAM, set your context size, and turn on LAN access so everyone at home can use it.

What Do You Need to Run a Local AI at Home?

Not much (other than the hardware). Here's a short list:

  • A Windows PC with a graphics card (GPU). The more video memory (VRAM) it has, the bigger the model it can run. I'm using an RTX 5090 with 32GB VRAM for this setup.
  • A free app that 'serves' the AI model to you through a chat interface. Get it from Unsloth.
  • An AI model sized to fit your GPU. We'll pick one in the next section.

That's it. No terminal commands, Python environments, or subscriptions required.

Which AI Model Can Your GPU Run?

It depends on how much VRAM your graphics card has. As a rough guide, 8-12GB of VRAM handles smaller 9B-12B models, while 32GB comfortably runs 27B-35B models with plenty of room for long conversations.

On consumer-grade hardware, we'll need smaller models. The full-size Qwen model sits at around 56GB and won't really fit on a consumer graphics card unless you're running a Mac with unified memory. That's where quantization comes in.

Quantization shrinks a model by compressing weights and moving to a lower precision. You basically trade some accuracy for a model that actually fits on your GPU and runs faster.

The same photo stored at 8, 4 and 2 bits per pixel. A model's weights lose detail the same way going from Q8 to Q4 to Q2.

If you're wondering whether this tradeoff is worth it, well, it depends. You'll find that certain types of workloads don't really care and give similar outputs, while others may be nearly unusable.

Which Model Should You Run for Your VRAM?

For this guide, we'll be going with Qwen3.8-27B with 4-bit quantization on my system with an RTX 5090. Going up a tier is an option thanks to its 32GB of VRAM, but I wanted to allow for a larger context window (how much of the conversation the model can keep in mind at once) rather than cramming in the largest model that fits.

Qwen3.8-27B at each precision with a 128K context, from our VRAM calculator. At 4-bit, the model and the context fit a 32 GB card with room to spare.

If you want to run a model of this caliber with excellent performance, a hilariously overpriced RTX 5090 (remember when $1,999 felt too high?) is unfortunately still not a terrible 'deal' these days. The other option is way more expensive enterprise-grade GPUs.

If you're on a GPU with less VRAM, you can still get something very usable going right away. The table below gives you a rough idea of where you can start.

Models marked MoE (mixture of experts) only run a few billion of their parameters for each token. They keep a decent speed on a smaller card with the rest held in system RAM, which is why a 35B model sits in the 16 GB row. On an RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, our calculator puts Qwen3.6-35B at about 47 tokens per second this way.

Feel free to experiment with several models until you find one that fits your needs. You can also use GPUPartner's VRAM Calculator to get an estimate.

Can You Run Inkling 2 on an RTX 5090?

Inkling 2 Mini, yes. Inkling 2 Small, no.

Inkling 2 Mini is the newest model in this size class. Thinking Machines Lab released it on November 17, 2026: 26.4B parameters, Apache 2.0, vision support and a 1M-token context. Unsloth's recommended file, UD-Q4_K_XL, is 17.6 GB. That is within 0.1 GB of the Qwen3.8-27B file in this guide, so it sits on a 32GB card the same way and leaves about 14GB for context.

Nothing else in this guide changes. Update Unsloth Desktop first, because Inkling 2 needs a recent build, then search for Inkling 2 Mini in the same drop-down in Step 2.

Those figures are Unsloth's. They count RAM and VRAM together and cover the model alone, so a long context needs more. Inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 5.4B parameters active, so the 4-bit file also runs on a 16 GB card with the remainder in system RAM, a little slower.

Can You Run a Local AI on a Mac?

Yes. You'll find good alternatives in Apple's Mac lineup thanks to its unified memory. Macs are pretty good at running larger models, even if they don't offer the best performance. Just make sure you grab the MLX flavor that is custom-built for Apple Silicon.

How Do You Set Up a Local AI with Unsloth Desktop?

It takes three steps: install Unsloth Desktop, download your model, and set the context size. I'll go over these steps in more detail below so you can follow along.

Step 1: Install Unsloth Desktop

First, we'll need a solution that 'serves' the AI model to you. My pursuit of simplicity narrowed my choices down to LM Studio or Unsloth Desktop. Both abstract away a ton of terminal commands and handle Python environments and dependencies behind a nice, simple UI, which makes them excellent picks for a first home setup.

I landed on Unsloth Desktop mostly because, well, I liked the name better. Also, it didn't try to push the very thing I was trying to escape when I opened its website: a subscription.

The community seems to like it overall too, so that's another point in its favor.

Once you've clicked through the installer and launched Unsloth, you'll see a window like this one.

Unsloth Desktop on first launch, before any model is loaded.

Step 2: Download a Quantized Model

On the top left of this main window, you can pick the model that you want to use from the drop down. We'll be using Qwen3.8-27B.

The model picker. Qwen3.8-27B is first on the Recommended list.

You should see a submenu like the one below when you click on a model. I'll be using Unsloth's UD-Q4_K_XL version. The M and S versions are smaller, but the XL version behaves much closer to the full-size model without filling up our VRAM, so it seemed like a good pick for my GPU.

Every quantization of Qwen3.8-27B with its download size. The gear next to the downloaded one holds the context setting.

Step 3: Set the Context Size

Once the download completes, you should see a gear icon to the right of the model as shown in the screenshot above. Here, you can set your context size manually or leave it on Auto if you aren't sure how much you need.

I'll be setting mine to 128K (unquantized) and might reassess after I've run the model through a few of my routine tasks for a few weeks. Again, you can use this VRAM calculator to help you with these numbers for your specific GPU.

At this point, our first local AI is up and running, and you can start chatting with it right inside Unsloth.

Remember, your mileage may vary depending on your setup.

How Do You Share a Local AI Across Your Home Network?

Short answer: Unsloth Desktop has LAN sharing built in. Set a Remote password, start LAN access, and share the address it gives you with anyone on your home network.

Once Unsloth Desktop is set up with a model, you might want to give family members or friends access too. For now, we'll only serve it over our local network, so my family can use it without needing physical access to this PC.

Head into Unsloth Desktop settings (gear icon on bottom left), and look for the 'Remote & LAN' tab.

Settings, Remote & LAN. LAN access is the second card. The Remote access card above it is for a later part.

Most of this section will be greyed out until you set a Remote password. Once you've set a password, you'll see a 'Start' button for LAN access. Click that and you should see an address that anyone on your home network can open in a browser to use a local AI model within a chat interface. They'll sign in as 'unsloth' with the Remote password you set.

Just keep in mind that the PC needs to stay on with Unsloth running for anyone to reach it.

Can You Access Your Local AI Across the Internet? Soon™

Not with this setup alone. Everything so far is limited to your local home network.

If you just need a chat interface like ChatGPT, Gemini, etc. to work within your home network, you're basically done at this point! You and anyone on your network can start talking to an AI model hosted on your machine right away.

In the next parts, we'll cover performance, tunneling, as well as setting up an agent that runs locally and uses only the web tools you allow it to use. This will let you automate more complex tasks like coding, research, and so much more without being tied to a subscription or usage limits and censorship.

As always, my focus remains simplicity that allows my family to use it without too much guidance or help.

PS. If you have any recommendations for agentic harnesses or even models to try, feel free to let me know and I'll give them a go!
